title: xv6 Internals: Traps, Scheduling and Sleep/Wakeup

sections.heading: Traps: From scause to usertrap
sections.body:
A trap is any event that forces a RISC-V hart from user mode into supervisor mode: a system call (the `ecall` instruction), an exception (illegal instruction, a misaligned or faulting load/store), or a device interrupt. The hardware records why in `scause`, the faulting program counter in `sepc`, the previous privilege level in the `SPP` bit of `sstatus`, copies `SIE` into `SPIE` to disable further interrupts, and jumps to the address in `stvec`. Deciding what the trap means is entirely software.

xv6-riscv keeps that software in one page of code, `trampoline.S`, mapped at the identical virtual address in the kernel's page table and in every process's user page table. That identical mapping is what makes the transition possible at all: for the first few instructions after a trap, `satp` (the page-table-base register) still points at the *user* page table, so the handler's own code must be visible under both mappings, or the hart would fault fetching it.

The user-mode entry point, `uservec`, saves all 32 general-purpose registers into a per-process *trapframe* page, loads the kernel's `satp`, the process's kernel stack pointer and the address of the C function `usertrap` — values the kernel stashed there in advance — then jumps into `usertrap`, now running on a normal kernel stack. `usertrap` reads `scause`: an environment call from U-mode advances `sepc` by 4 (past the `ecall`) and dispatches through the system-call table; anything else is an exception or a device interrupt, handled by code shared with traps taken while already in the kernel. `usertrapret` prepares the reverse trip — refreshing the trapframe, setting `SPP=0` and `SPIE=1` so the return lands in user mode with interrupts back on — and hands off to `userret`, which restores the 32 user registers, switches `satp` back to the user page table, and executes `sret`.

sections.heading: The Per-CPU Scheduler Loop and swtch
sections.body:
Every hart runs its own instance of `scheduler()`, an infinite loop over the fixed-size process table: for each `RUNNABLE` process it acquires that process's lock, marks it `RUNNING`, records it as `mycpu()->proc`, and calls `swtch(&c->context, &p->context)`. Control does not return to the loop until some later trap or voluntary yield switches back to this hart's own context, at which point `scheduler()` releases the lock and starts the scan again.

`swtch` is a short leaf routine, not a general register-saving mechanism: the RISC-V calling convention already guarantees that a function call clobbers only the caller-saved registers, so the only state a context switch needs to preserve across a call/return boundary is the callee-saved set — `ra`, `sp`, and `s0` through `s11`, fourteen 8-byte slots in `struct context`. There is no separate saved program counter: the saved `ra` *is* the resume address, so returning from `swtch` with a swapped register file is indistinguishable from a genuine context switch. Floating-point registers are untouched, because the kernel itself never uses them.

`sched()`, the wrapper every blocking path calls, checks its own invariants first — the caller must already hold exactly its own `p->lock`, interrupts must be disabled, `p->state` must not be `RUNNING` — then calls `swtch(&p->context, &mycpu()->context)` to hand the hart back to that CPU's scheduler loop. `yield()` is the thinnest client of this machinery: acquire `p->lock`, set `RUNNABLE`, call `sched()`, and only after some later `swtch` resumes this process does `yield()` release the lock.

sections.heading: Sleep, Wakeup and the Lost-Wakeup Race
sections.body:
`sleep(chan, lk)` and `wakeup(chan)` implement the address-keyed rendezvous inherited from BSD Unix: a process waiting for some event calls `sleep` on the address of whatever it is waiting for (a buffer header, a pipe, a child's exit status), and whoever makes that event true calls `wakeup` on the same address, which moves every process sleeping on it back to `RUNNABLE`. No queue object is allocated per condition — the address itself is the key, and `wakeup` finds waiters by scanning the whole process table.

That design is only correct because of a specific hand-off. Naively, "check the condition, and if false, sleep" is two separate steps, and a wakeup landing in the gap between them is lost forever — exactly what the classic producer-consumer example (a shared `count`, with unprotected `sleep()` and `wakeup(consumer)` calls) demonstrates: the consumer reads `count == 0`, is preempted before it can mark itself asleep, the producer runs to completion and calls `wakeup` while the consumer is still merely `RUNNABLE`, so the wakeup has nobody to find, and both sides eventually block forever.

xv6 closes the gap by requiring the caller to already hold `lk`, the lock that protects the condition being tested, and by never letting the condition go unprotected: `sleep` first acquires `p->lock` (skipping this step only if `lk` already *is* `p->lock`), *then* releases `lk`, then sets `p->chan = chan` and `p->state = SLEEPING`, and only then calls `sched()`. Because `p->lock` is held continuously from before `lk` is dropped until after the state flips to `SLEEPING`, and because `wakeup` must acquire that same `p->lock` before it may even read `p->state`, no concurrent wakeup can land in a gap where the sleeper has decided to block but not yet recorded it.

sections.heading: Spinlocks on RISC-V: acquire, release, push_off
sections.body:
A `struct spinlock` is a single `locked` word plus debugging fields. `acquire()` first calls `push_off()`, which disables interrupts on the current hart and increments a per-CPU nesting counter, remembering — only on the outermost call — whether interrupts were enabled beforehand. It then spins: `while (__sync_lock_test_and_set(&lk->locked, 1) != 0) ;`. The RISC-V backend lowers that GCC builtin to a single atomic swap instruction (`amoswap.w`, acquire-ordered), not a separate load and store — exactly the ingredient missing from a naive lock built out of a plain `while(held); held = 1;`, where the test and the set are two instructions with a window between them for another hart to slip through. A full fence (`__sync_synchronize()`) follows, ordering the critical section after the acquire. `release()` mirrors this: fence, then an atomic release-store of 0, then `pop_off()`, which only re-enables interrupts once the nesting counter returns to zero.

Disabling interrupts locally is not about the atomic instruction's correctness — it is about a specific self-deadlock: if a timer interrupt fires on the same hart that is spinning for, or holding, the lock, and the interrupt path tries to acquire that same lock or invoke the scheduler, that hart wants a lock it will never release. Turning off interrupts on that hart for the critical section's duration removes that possibility; it says nothing about a different hart also spinning, the ordinary cost of contention. This is also why spinlocks are meant to be held only briefly, and why holding one across a call that can block — `sleep`, in particular — is forbidden everywhere except the one sanctioned case, `p->lock`, which the scheduler and `sched()` are written to hand off across `swtch` itself.

sections.heading: Why the Sleep/Wakeup Hand-off Is Race-Free
sections.body:
State the invariant precisely: every write to `p->state` and `p->chan` happens with `p->lock` held — inside `sleep`, `sched`, `wakeup` and `yield` alike — and every actor that can make the condition true must itself hold `lk` (that is what "the lock that protects the condition" means as a convention). Consider the interval from the moment a sleeping process last re-checks the condition, under `lk`, to the moment it finishes setting `p->state = SLEEPING`, under `p->lock`. By construction `sleep` never drops both locks at once inside this interval: it holds `lk` right up to the point where it has acquired `p->lock`, and only then releases `lk`, so at least one of the two locks is held throughout.

Any concurrent process that flips the condition must hold `lk` to do so, so its own critical section runs entirely before or entirely after this interval — it cannot straddle it, because `lk` is exclusive. If it runs *before*, the sleeper's own re-check, taken under `lk` immediately before calling `sleep`, already observes the new condition and skips sleeping. If it runs *after*, the sleeper is already `SLEEPING` with `p->chan` set, and any `wakeup` call on that channel — which must acquire `p->lock` before it may even compare `p->chan` — is serialized after the state flip and will find it. There is no third case, because the interval is never left with both locks free at once.

sections.heading: Trade-offs: Scan vs Queue, Fairness, the Trampoline Trick
sections.body:
`wakeup(chan)`'s cost is proportional to the size of the process table, not to the number of actual waiters — every process, sleeping or not, on this channel or not, is examined. Linux's `wait_queue_head_t`, used with `wait_event()`/`wake_up()`, instead threads each waiting task onto an explicit list rooted at the condition itself, so waking costs time proportional to the actual waiters, at the price of maintaining that list under its own lock and re-deriving the same lock-then-check-then-sleep contract xv6 solves with the `lk`/`p->lock` hand-off; the hazard is identical, only the data structure that avoids it differs.

xv6's spinlock is simple in a way that costs something too: a bare `amoswap`-based test-and-set gives no fairness guarantee, so an unlucky hart can in principle lose every race for a heavily contended lock. Ticket locks — an atomic fetch-and-add hands out a ticket, and a spinner waits until a "now serving" counter reaches its own number — restore FIFO order at the cost of one more atomic per acquire.

The trampoline page is xv6's specific answer to a narrower problem: the instant of the `satp` switch cannot also be the instant of an instruction-stream discontinuity, or the fetch right after the switch would fault under the new page table. Mapping one page of code identically everywhere sidesteps that question. xv6's flat round-robin `scheduler()`, with no priority field anywhere in `struct proc`, is a simplification made for the same pedagogical reasons, standing in deliberate contrast to the priority queues and multilevel feedback schemes the course covers separately.

complexity.space: 1 trapframe page + 1 kernel stack per process
complexity.notes: Trampoline page mapped identically in every address space

complexity.space: $O(1)$, one `struct context` per process and per CPU
complexity.notes: No FP or caller-saved registers touched; resumes via `ret` to the saved `ra`
Holds `p->lock` only for the candidate currently being inspected
`lk` is released only after `p->lock` is already held
Scans every process regardless of how many actually wait on `chan`

complexity.time: $O(1)$: one `amoswap` plus one fence, each way

code.caption: pthreads producer-consumer using a mutex + condition variables, the same lock-then-check-then-wait protocol as xv6's sleep(chan, lk)/wakeup(chan); compiled and run repeatedly, always prints sum = 15.

worked_example.problem: Two kernel threads share a bounded buffer of capacity 1 and a variable `count`, guarded only by the classic *unprotected* pattern: `if (count == 0) sleep(); ... wakeup(producer);` in the consumer and `if (count == N) sleep(); ... wakeup(consumer);` in the producer — no lock covers the check-then-sleep step. Trace an interleaving of Producer P and Consumer C, starting from `count = 0`, that makes both threads block forever. Then show why xv6's `sleep(chan, lk)` protocol, which requires the caller to hold the buffer's lock across that same check, closes exactly this gap.
worked_example.solution:
**The race (unprotected sleep/wakeup).** Start with `count = 0`.

| Step | Thread | Action | `count` after |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | C | reads `count == 0` → true, decides to sleep | 0 |
| T1 | — | C is preempted *before* it calls `sleep()` | 0 |
| T2 | P | produces an item, `insert_item()`, `count = 0 + 1 = 1` | 1 |
| T3 | P | `count == 1` → calls `wakeup(consumer)` | 1 |
| T4 | — | C is not yet `SLEEPING` (its state is still whatever it was at T0), so `wakeup` finds no one on this channel — the wakeup is lost | 1 |
| T5 | C | resumes and executes the `sleep()` it had already committed to at T0, based on the now-stale `count == 0` test | 1 |
| T6 | P | eventually fills the buffer (`count == N`), also calls `sleep()`, waiting for a `wakeup(producer)` only C can send | 1 |

C is asleep waiting for a `wakeup(consumer)` that already fired and vanished; P is asleep waiting for a `wakeup(producer)` that only a running consumer could send. Neither will ever run again — both `sleep()` calls block forever.

**Why holding the lock across the gap fixes it.** Replace the pattern with xv6's `sleep(chan, lk)`, where `lk` is the mutex that already protects `count`. T0 and T1 can no longer be split the same way: C's check of `count == 0` happens with `lk` held, and `sleep` does not release `lk` until it has first acquired its own `p->lock` and recorded `p->state = SLEEPING`. P cannot touch `count` or call `wakeup` without first acquiring `lk` itself, so P's entire insert-and-wakeup sequence is serialized either strictly before C's check (C's check under `lk` then already sees `count == 1` and skips sleeping) or strictly after C is already marked `SLEEPING` (`wakeup`'s scan, which itself takes `p->lock`, finds C). The interleaving at T1 that stranded the wakeup between "decided to sleep" and "recorded as asleep" is no longer schedulable, because a lock P cannot bypass now covers that window.

The compiled listing in `code.source` implements exactly this fixed protocol with a capacity-1 buffer and five items; run repeatedly (verified five times in a row on this machine) it always terminates with `sum = 1+2+3+4+5 = 15`, unlike the buggy version, which can hang.

pitfalls: **Checking, then sleeping, unlocked.** Splitting "test the condition" and "call sleep" without a lock covering both reopens the exact lost-wakeup race `sleep(chan, lk)` exists to close.

**`if` instead of `while` around the wait.** `wakeup(chan)` moves *every* sleeper on that channel to `RUNNABLE`, not just the intended one, and the condition can be false again by the time this thread actually runs; always re-check after waking.

**Holding a spinlock across a blocking call.** Any spinlock held across `sleep` or another blocking operation deadlocks the system, since nothing else can ever make progress to release it — the sole exception is `p->lock`, held across `swtch` by design.

**Treating `swtch` as saving "the process's state".** It saves only the callee-saved integer registers (`ra`, `sp`, `s0`–`s11`); anything already spilled under the caller-saved convention, and any floating-point state, is not part of `struct context`.

**Assuming every trap goes through `uservec`.** A trap taken while already running kernel code (a timer interrupt during a system call) is vectored through `kernelvec`/`kerneltrap` instead, which is set as `stvec` only while the kernel is running.
**Forgetting that `push_off`/`pop_off` nest.** Calling `pop_off` after only some of several nested `acquire()` calls re-enables interrupts too early, mid critical section.
applications: **BSD Unix's `tsleep()`/`wakeup()`.** The direct ancestor of xv6's address-keyed rendezvous, including the original single-CPU fix of raising hardware processor priority instead of a per-condition lock.
**Linux `wait_queue_head_t` + `wait_event()`/`wake_up()`.** Same lock-then-check-then-sleep contract, implemented with an explicit per-condition queue instead of a whole-table scan.

**POSIX condition variables (`pthread_cond_wait`/`pthread_cond_signal`).** The user-space version of the same hand-off, which is why the fixed producer-consumer code here is a line-for-line analogue of xv6's `sleep`/`wakeup`.
**`local_irq_save`/`splhigh`-style interrupt masking in production kernels.** The same push-off-before-spin discipline xv6 uses, to stop a hart from deadlocking against its own interrupt handler.
**RISC-V Linux's kernel entry path (`entry.S`).** The same trap-frame save/restore and `sret`-based return-to-user structure as xv6's trampoline, at production scale.
exam_focus: The assigned OSTEP reading includes Figure 6.4, captioned "The xv6 Context Switch Code" — students are expected to read and trace a real `swtch()` listing register by register, not just cite its cost as O(1).

The assigned Silberschatz Appendix C excerpt on BSD UNIX frames sleep()/wakeup() as an address-keyed rendezvous and explicitly names the race it can suffer, attributing the original single-CPU fix to raising hardware processor priority — the course expects a contrast with a lock-based, SMP-safe fix.

Producer/consumer is taught with Tanenbaum's count-based sleep()/wakeup() example and its "fatal race condition"; the same count/insert_item/wakeup(consumer) shape recurs verbatim across the slides, so a lost-wakeup question is likely to use this exact notation rather than condition variables.

The spinlock slides build a naive lock in visible steps (busy-wait test, the unprotected held=1 write, "what if a context switch happens here?") and pair it with a live counter-race demo — expect a question asking where the race is and why an atomic instruction or disabled interrupts, not a bigger loop, fixes it.

self_check.question: Why must `sleep(chan, lk)` be called with `lk` already held, instead of checking the condition unlocked and then calling a plain `sleep(chan)`?
self_check.answer: Because "check the condition" and "record yourself as asleep" are two separate operations, and if nothing holds them together, a wakeup can be sent in the gap between them and be lost forever — the process is not yet `SLEEPING`, so `wakeup`'s scan finds nothing to do, and the call has no lasting effect. `sleep(chan, lk)` closes that gap by requiring `lk` — the lock that already protects the condition — to be held across the check, and by not releasing `lk` until it has first acquired its own `p->lock` and set `p->state = SLEEPING`. Any process that could change the condition and call `wakeup` must also acquire `lk` first, so it cannot run inside that gap: either it runs before the sleeper's last check (which then sees the new value and never sleeps) or after the sleeper is already marked `SLEEPING` (which `wakeup`'s table scan, itself gated by `p->lock`, will find). Passing an unlocked or wrong lock to `sleep` reopens exactly this race.

self_check.question: `struct context` in xv6-riscv holds `ra`, `sp` and `s0`–`s11` (each 8 bytes on RV64). A workload issues 10,000 system calls, each of which calls `yield()` exactly once (one `swtch()` call per yield, switching the process out to the scheduler). How many register saves-and-restores does `swtch` perform in total across the workload, and how many bytes of register state does it move, counting both the save and the restore side of each call?
self_check.answer: `struct context` has `ra`, `sp`, and `s0` through `s11` — 2 + 12 = 14 registers, each 8 bytes, so 112 bytes are saved from the old context and 112 bytes loaded into the new one: 224 bytes moved per `swtch()` call. Over 10,000 yields that is $10000 \times 14 = 140000$ register saves-and-restores in total, moving $10000 \times 224 = 2240000$ bytes — about 2.14 MiB of register traffic. This is cheap compared to a full trap round trip, which additionally saves all 32 user registers into the trapframe and switches `satp` twice.

self_check.question: `wakeup(chan)` scans the entire process table on every call, whether or not anyone is waiting on `chan`. Give its cost in terms of the process-table size $P$ and the number of actual waiters $W$, describe one alternative design that would make the cost depend on $W$ instead, and name the price that design pays in return.
self_check.answer: `wakeup(chan)`'s cost is $O(P)$ regardless of $W$ — it has no way to know in advance which, if any, of the $P$ table slots are sleeping on `chan`, so it inspects every one, acquiring and releasing that process's lock to compare `p->chan`. An alternative is a per-condition wait queue — a linked list of exactly the waiting threads, rooted at the condition itself, as Linux's `wait_queue_head_t` does — which turns `wake_up()` into an $O(W)$ walk of just the actual waiters. The price is bookkeeping: every sleep/`wait_event()` call must now splice itself onto that list under the queue's own lock and remove itself again on every exit path, including the less common ones (a signal, a timeout) — exactly the extra state and extra lock that xv6 avoids by making every channel an untyped address with no list at all. For a process table sized in the tens to low hundreds, as in a teaching kernel, the $O(P)$ scan is cheap enough that the simplicity is the better trade.

key_points: A trap saves scause/sepc/sstatus, runs uservec→usertrap, and returns via usertrapret→userret→sret.
swtch() saves only ra, sp and s0–s11 (14 registers) — the resume point is the saved ra, not a stored PC.
sleep(chan, lk) must hold lk until it holds p->lock, or a concurrent wakeup(chan) can be lost.
wakeup(chan) scans the whole process table — it is not a per-channel queue, so its cost is O(P).
acquire() disables local interrupts (push_off) before spinning on an atomic swap, to avoid self-deadlock.
xv6's scheduler is flat round-robin — no priority field, unlike the MLFQ schemes covered separately.
tagline: xv6 traps flip privilege via scause/sepc; swtch saves 14 registers; sleep(chan,lk) must hold lk until it holds p->lock, or a wakeup is lost.
tldr: xv6 handles a trap by saving RISC-V's `scause`/`sepc`/`sstatus` into a trapframe and running `uservec → usertrap → usertrapret → userret`, a round trip that switches `satp` twice through a trampoline page mapped identically in every address space. Each hart's `scheduler()` picks a `RUNNABLE` process and calls `swtch()`, a leaf routine that saves only the 14 callee-saved registers (`ra`, `sp`, `s0`–`s11`); the saved `ra` is what makes "returning" into a context switch. `sleep(chan, lk)`/`wakeup(chan)` implement a BSD-style address-keyed rendezvous, correct only because `sleep` hands off from `lk` to `p->lock` without ever leaving the condition unprotected — the classic lost-wakeup race this design exists to close. Spinlocks add one more piece: disabling local interrupts before spinning on an atomic `amoswap`, since a spinlock may never be held across a voluntary sleep.
